meta.title: Who really said "In all things of nature there is something of the marvelous"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Aristotle really wrote the sentence — Parts of Animals I.5, 645a — but this popular English wording matches no published translation we could locate.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In all things of nature there is something of the marvelous'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Aristotle, real passage (Parts of Animals I.5, 645a) — but the famous English belongs to no translator we can name. Ogle and Peck both word it differently.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher and the first systematic biologist
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Aristotle’s and the sentence is locatable: it sits in Parts of Animals, Book I, chapter 5 (Bekker 645a16–17), where the Greek reads “ἐν πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἔνεστί τι θαυμαστόν.” What we could not pin down is this exact English. W. Ogle’s 1882 translation compresses the clause into “Every realm of nature is marvellous”; A. L. Peck’s 1937 Loeb has “in all natural things there is somewhat of the marvellous.” The popular wording matches no published translation we could locate, and the sites that carry it cite no edition at all.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Parts of Animals (De Partibus Animalium), Book I, chapter 5
Excerpt below: W. Ogle, Aristotle on the Parts of Animals (London: Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., 1882). Compare A. L. Peck, Loeb Classical Library (1937).
Attributed — the passage is Aristotle’s, but this exact English belongs to no translation we could identify

source.excerpt: We therefore must not recoil with childish aversion from the examination of the humbler animals. Every realm of nature is marvellous: and as Heraclitus, when the strangers who came to visit him found him warming himself at the furnace in the kitchen, is reported to have bidden them not to be afraid to enter, as even in that kitchen divinities were present, so we should venture on the study of every kind of animal without distaste; for each and all will reveal to us something natural and something beautiful.
trail: The clause is where the Greek says it is. In the Loeb Classical Library Parts of Animals, the Greek at 645a runs “ἐν πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἔνεστί τι θαυμαστόν,” and A. L. Peck’s facing English reads “since in all natural things there is somewhat of the marvellous” (full text of the volume ↗). The Wellcome Collection catalogue dates that Loeb volume to 1937, Heinemann and Harvard University Press ↗.

The oldest English of the passage says something different. W. Ogle’s translation — published by Kegan Paul, Trench & Co. in 1882 ↗ — compresses the clause to “Every realm of nature is marvellous ↗.” A reader looking for the popular sentence in the standard public-domain translation will never find it.

Modern scholarship words it a third way. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Aristotle’s biology ↗, by James G. Lennox, quotes the passage as PA I 5, 645a4–36 and renders the line “For in all natural things there is something marvelous” — close to the circulating version, but not identical, and the entry names no translator for it.

The popular wording travels without a source. On Wikiquote ↗ it appears only as an uncited caption beneath an engraving, while the page’s sourced Parts of Animals entry (Book I, Part 5) uses Ogle’s wording; Goodreads ↗ and the other aggregators give the author’s name and nothing else.
source.excerptNote: That is W. Ogle’s 1882 rendering, transcribed from the scanned Kegan Paul edition. The clause behind the famous quote is the one Ogle turns into “Every realm of nature is marvellous”; Peck’s 1937 Loeb, printed facing the Greek, gives it as “in all natural things there is somewhat of the marvellous.”

source.rightsNote: Aristotle’s Greek has been out of copyright for centuries, and the translation excerpted above — W. Ogle’s, published in 1882 — is public domain in the United States ↗. The status of the popular one-line wording itself is a separate question and cannot be settled here: it is not Ogle’s, and it is not the wording of A. L. Peck’s 1937 Loeb translation (which remains in copyright), so we cannot say which edition, if any, it came from.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Aristotle
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher and the first systematic biologist
author.bio: Aristotle joined Plato’s Academy in Athens at about seventeen and stayed close to twenty years; later, barred as a foreigner from owning property, he rented the buildings known as the Lyceum and ran his own school there. Biology takes up a large share of his surviving work — History of Animals, Generation of Animals, Parts of Animals — and much of it rests on first-hand observation, including a stretch of zoological fieldwork around Lesbos. Parts of Animals is where he stops mid-treatise to argue that the humblest creature repays study, and this sentence is the hinge of that argument.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this one. The name on the card is right, and so is the sentiment — the problem is that the exact English has no parent, and the sites that spread it never say where it came from.

items.why: The two standard English versions of the passage both say something else. Ogle’s 1882 translation reads “Every realm of nature is marvellous ↗”; A. L. Peck’s Loeb reads “in all natural things there is somewhat of the marvellous ↗.” The circulating sentence is a third rendering with no translator’s name attached to it.

Goodreads, BrainyQuote, Quotefancy and the rest carry the line with the author’s name and nothing else — no work, no book, no translator. Goodreads even prints a disclaimer ↗ that its quotes are community-added and not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence itself is real Aristotle: Parts of Animals I.5, Bekker 645a16–17, part of his argument that even the humblest animal repays study — read the passage in context ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Aristotle wrote this in the middle of a defence — of himself, and of the whole business of dissecting animals. He has just conceded that some creatures are unpleasant to look at, and that studying the heavens is in one sense the nobler pursuit. His answer is that we can actually get at the causes of things down here, and that a bloody, unglamorous specimen on the bench is still nature doing something worth understanding.

To make the point stick he tells a story about Heraclitus, found by visitors warming himself at the kitchen stove: embarrassed, they hung back, and he told them to come in anyway, because there were gods in there too. Aristotle’s conclusion, in Ogle’s 1882 English, is that we should “venture on the study of every kind of animal without distaste; for each and all will reveal to us something natural and something beautiful.” It is a manifesto for field biology, written in a treatise dated to around 350 BC.
detailsBody: The Greek clause is short — seven words — and translators have split on how literally to take it. Ogle turned it into an aphorism (“Every realm of nature is marvellous”). Peck, working for a facing-page Loeb edition, stayed closer to the syntax (“in all natural things there is somewhat of the marvellous”). The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s article on Aristotle’s biology ↗, citing PA I 5, 645a4–36, renders it “For in all natural things there is something marvelous.”

The circulating quote-card version sits closest to that last shape, with “all natural things” smoothed into “all things of nature.” That is a reasonable rendering of the Greek — it is simply not one we can trace to a translator, a publisher or a date, which is why this page stops short of calling it verified.
context.pull: Every realm of nature is marvellous.
